On a cold Saturday in March, the Northfield Rovers travelled to Bracken Park knowing that a single point would keep their promotion hopes alive. The visitors had lost three of their previous four matches, and their manager, Alison Frayne, had spent the week rebuilding a midfield that had looked ragged since the winter break. Bracken's pitch was heavy, the wind came in gusts off the river, and the home supporters arrived early to fill the terrace behind the goal.

The first half offered little to warm anyone. Bracken pressed high, forcing the Rovers to play long, and the ball spent most of its time in the air. Twice the home side won corners, and twice the keeper punched clear. Frayne stood at the edge of her technical area, arms folded, watching the shape of her team drift apart. At the interval she gathered the players in the changing room and told them to keep their passes short and their tempers shorter.

The second half began better. A through ball from the left found the striker, who turned inside the full back and drew a save that the crowd greeted with a groan. Then, in the fifty-eighth minute, the match turned. Bracken's captain went down under a challenge near the halfway line and stayed down, clutching his ankle. The referee stopped play, the physio ran on, and after several minutes the captain was helped to the touchline. The home side, suddenly a man short in midfield, lost their rhythm.

Frayne later described the situation in which her team found itself as the turning point of the season. With Bracken unsettled, the Rovers pushed forward, and within ten minutes a low cross from the right was turned in at the far post. The goal was scrappy, deflected twice, but it counted. Later, the club's sports scientists tracked the effects of the altitude camp on the players' recovery times, and their report shaped the training plan for the following month. Bracken threw on two substitutes and pressed for an equaliser, and for a while the Rovers defended desperately, clearing balls off the line and blocking shots with whatever part of the body was nearest.

When the final whistle came, the travelling fans spilled toward the fence and sang until the stewards asked them to move along. Frayne shook hands with the opposing manager and walked slowly back down the tunnel. A draw away from home, on a heavy pitch, with a depleted squad, was not the result her critics had predicted. In the press room she was careful not to overstate it. There were still nine matches to play, she said, and the table would look different by May. Two of the injured players were expected back within a fortnight, which helped. But she allowed herself a small smile as she left.
